    October 2026

    • Treasury is a social job
    • More interim roles in finance?

    During the last years, I saw much demand for full remote or hybrid positions in treasury, and I have to say that I am probably more pro office than the current trend.

    Part of it is simply personal. I focus better in an office. I like being surrounded by people working on the same things, being able to walk into somebody's office with a question, discuss something for five minutes, or sometimes just have a conversation that has nothing to do with work. For me, all of that somehow keeps me more connected to the job.

    But I also think there is something particular about treasury.

    Treasury is obviously based on numbers. We calculate NPV, IRR, funding costs, risks, returns and plenty of other things. But it is not an exact science. I remember one CFO saying that every important decision needed to be looked at from three sides: economic, tax and legal. And once you put all three together, things are rarely completely black or white.

    Anyone who has worked with lawyers knows what I mean. There is a clause, an interpretation, something that is not entirely clear... and eventually management has to make a decision. The same happens with tax, accounting, negotiations and risk. Sometimes all point in one direction and an experienced CFO still says that something doesn't feel right. He had a gut feeling...

    How do you learn that?

    I think a lot of it comes from being around experienced people. Listening to discussions. Seeing how somebody negotiates with a bank. Watching how a CFO challenges a proposal. Having an informal conversation after a meeting. This is particularly important for junior professionals because part of learning treasury is simply learning the trade.

    That is why, at least today, I struggle with the idea of fully remote treasury teams. Hybrid working has obvious advantages to working from home. But if I were designing a treasury team, I would still give more weight to time together in the office.

    Maybe technology eventually changes my view. I can imagine something almost science fiction like: working from home but putting on a device and effectively entering a virtual office, where your colleagues are around you and conversations happen naturally rather than through scheduled Teams calls. At the speed technology is moving, perhaps that isn't even particularly science fiction anymore.

    If we ever get there, maybe the distinction between remote and office work becomes irrelevant.

    But we aren't there yet. And for now I still think treasury is a social job.
